utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber notices that Mr. Simo Zaric is not in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Zaric has a minor dental surgery today. He signed his waiver yesterday, and he waived his right to be here today. And we can proceed without his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can proceed without him. Okay. It was cross-examination, I think. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Tubakovic. Can Mr. Tubakovic be provided with a statement of his --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tubakovic. Sorry. With a copy of his statement in B/C/S. It's D184/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, please be polite to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was trying to correct my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You better be civilised. That's all. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if it came across that way. It certainly was not intended in any uncivilised way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, do you have your statement there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday just before we broke I was asking you about a statement you made in paragraph 23 in which you said, "There were no telephone lines for a long time and I know this myself because I wanted to send a fax in connection with work." Just have a look at that, please. That's what's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you agreed with me yesterday you didn't know whether the phones were working at the SUP, the civil protection, the municipal building, or the Crisis Staff, you just didn't know. That was your evidence yesterday. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have positively asserted in your statement that telephones were out of operation for all citizens, haven't you? It's a positive assertion.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic -- sorry, I'm going to have difficulties with his pronunciation. I just wish to say I'm going to have some difficulties in pronouncing it, and I'm not in any way attempting to denigrate the witness by -- if I hesitate or pause in my pronunciation. It's just a difficulty I'm going to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's understandable. You're not familiar with the names, but Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tubakovic; is that correct? Tubakovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's maybe easier if I call you "sir." Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's better perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a positive assertion there, sir, that the telephone lines were out of order for everyone, but you of course didn't work at the telephone exchange, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not work at the telephone exchange, but in my building and in town the citizens did not have any telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not trying to say that some authorities did not have any telephones. Most probably they did. My secretariat, the Secretariat for National Defence, did not have any telephone lines. Because of these telephone lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stop. My question was: You didn't work at the telephone exchange? Okay? The answer to that is no. And of course when you -- when your telephone line was reconnected --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When your telephone line was reconnected, you of course didn't telephone everyone in town to find out whether their line was working, did you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the telephone exchange is operating, then I know that lines are connected. I did not talk to all citizens, but those citizens I did talk to had telephones. I talked to my neighbour Mehmed Avdibegovic and Muhidin Halilovic, they had telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of talking to two people you can't say that the lines were cut for everyone, can you? That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other citizens also said that they did not have any telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll move on, sir. In paragraph 20 of your statement you refer to your wife having a work obligation. I just want you to briefly tell us in as few words as possible, what was your wife's work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's a salesperson. She was manager of a shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was her -- the work obligation she received during the war, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All citizens were assigned to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm asking you to --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was her work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the entirety of the war? That's what I asked you. Was that your wife's work obligation during the war? Just answer that one, please.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also referred in your statement to Mr. Tadic -- I'm sorry, you gave evidence of Mr. Tadic going to the communication centre and talking to Mr. Mijo Matanovic. Do you remember that evidence; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard him speaking over the radio to Mr. Matanovic. Was that in relation to the exchange of people from one side to the other?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is the reason why Mr. Tadic spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Tadic discussing with Mr. Matanovic the exchange of civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not at the communications centre often. This is separate from my office. These are different premises. But on a few occasions I had the opportunity of seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, please. My question -- please don't answer a different question. The question I asked you was: Did you hear Mr. Tadic discussing with Mr. Matanovic the exchange of civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Maybe we could just clarify. The witness's answer was, "I heard about that." Did he hear it himself or did he hear it from other persons? It's a little bit ambiguous there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will clarify that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, you said you heard about that. Are you saying you heard about it from hearing what Mr. Tadic was saying to Mr. Matanovic, that they were discussing the exchange of prisoners of war and civilians?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you also overhear Mr. Tadic talking to representatives of the 1st Krajina Corps, such as Milutin Grujicic about the exchange of prisoners of war and civilians?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that. No. At that time I was not at the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Mr. -- did you see Mr. Tadic discuss the exchange of prisoners of war and -- soldiers, prisoners of war, and civilians with Mr. Velimir Maslic or Mr. Svetozar Vasovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither Velimir Maslic nor Svetozar Vasovic came to the communications centre. I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence yesterday was of Mr. Tadic coming to your block of apartments with a soldier called Micic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mikic"]. That's what you told the Court yesterday, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I looked at the transcript. I think that the testimony said that first the soldier came and then Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is what the transcript says. If this is put to the witness, then I think it should be put correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't want to interrupt, but again, the name was misspelt on page 6, line 11. It's Micic and not Mikic, with C. M-i-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Yes. You've understood Mr. Lukic's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand the order of how they came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was a summary of the two, but I will put it in a completely more precise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, please don't look at your statement. Mr. Tubakovic, thank you, sir. I'm asking you about what you said yesterday in court. You said a soldier called Micic came downstairs, banged on the door, and Mr. Tadic came a few minutes later, and then Mr. Tadic and the soldier came up to the -- came up to the door of your apartment.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. First the soldier came, this Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was there was one soldier who accompanied Tadic. That was your evidence yesterday, wasn't it? Or one soldier who came before Mr. Tadic. That was your evidence yesterday, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tadic came to you -- came to the flat or the entrance to the flat, spoke to you, and people there, and he and the soldier Micic left shortly afterwards. That was your evidence yesterday, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence yesterday you said that -- I withdraw that. And your evidence yesterday was that there were only two of them. That was Micic and Mr. Tadic who came to your flat.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, when they came, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. Now, your evidence yesterday was that Mr. Tadic -- Mr. Lukic asked you yesterday about whether or not Mr. Tadic was armed. The question was -- this is at page 80: "Do you remember" -- at line 4 -- "if he had any weapons on him?" And your answer was, "No, he didn't. The soldier Micic did, but Tadic did not. He didn't have any weapons. He wasn't carrying a weapon in his hands or was it slung on his shoulder." That was your evidence yesterday, sir. You have your statement in front of you, sir. You agree that was your evidence yesterday, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please look at your statement, sir, paragraph 11 of your statement. I'm sorry. This is under seal, Your Honour. Could it just be taken off the ELMO. Could you just turn it over, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Wait a minute. It's redacted. I apologise. He's looking at something which has been redacted. I meant to show him the unredacted, which is D184/3. My error. And it is actually redacted, so I'd ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. For the paragraphs that were struck off, that's why they are redacted, so you can't refer to them. This is why the witness came to give viva voce evidence. On the basis of a prior statement, Your Honour, I will read to him what he said or I will show to him what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not a redacted paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, not in open session, Your Honour. That's the point. It's only redacted because of the person's name, not because of the contents. I'm putting something to him on the basis of a prior and consistent statement. The evidence he gave yesterday is different to what was in the statement he gave. Whether it's redacted or not has nothing to do with -- is irrelevant for the purposes of impeaching a witness as to a prior and consistent statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the Trial Chamber is of the view that you can't refer to anything in a paragraph which was struck off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is Your Honour telling me that I cannot cross-examine a witness as to his credibility based upon a prior statement he has made, signed, sworn, before a registry officer, which contains different evidence to the evidence which he gave yesterday? Yesterday he said something which is completely different to what is in the signed statement. I'm putting it as to his credibility under Rule 90(H) only on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think maybe we're just under a little bit of a misconception here. This -- these paragraphs are not redacted to protect any protected witnesses and so on. The Trial Chamber struck out these paragraphs when we analysed all of the 92 bis statements. And as our Presiding Judge Mumba has indicated, when we said which paragraphs were being struck out, it was because they referred specifically to the accused persons directly with respect to the indictment. So they shouldn't have been there in the first place. So we have not redacted them. We have struck them out and have allowed, therefore, examination-in-chief on those paragraphs, and obviously -- not on those paragraphs but on the issues contained in those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe there's a misunderstanding or confusion. I used the word "redacted" wrongly. I didn't mean redacted, and I withdraw that. The statement he made, that is, a prior statement. Whether it contains -- no matter when it was made, he has made a statement out of court which is different to the evidence he made in court. It is no different to a witness making a statement which the witness is entitled to be cross-examined on as to a different version of the same set of events. For the cross-examination -- for the Prosecutor to cross-examine this witness properly, because there is a conflict between the evidence of this witness and others as to his reliability and his veracity, the Prosecutor must be able to put to him a version he gave which is different a few weeks ago to the version he's given in court as to several very distinct matters. It is no different, in my submission, to the statement of any Prosecution witness which was given earlier and not in oral testimony which is different as to the acts or conduct of the accused. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you've been overruled. That is all. The Trial Chamber has overruled you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, I want to make an offer of proof on the transcript that the Trial Chamber has made a ruling which has prevented the Prosecution from cross-examining the witness as to inconsistencies between a prior version and the version given in court, and the Prosecution is unable to put its case or cross-examine the witness properly under Rule 90(H)(ii) as to the witness's credibility because the statements which were provided and were ID give a different version to the version given in court and the Prosecution will be unable to submit the witness -- anything in relation to the witness's veracity based upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Re, when they were given numbers for identification purposes only, they were not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just preserving the Prosecution's position for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At the time -- yes. At the time that the statements were admitted into evidence, the paragraphs that were struck out were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that that is no longer evidence which can be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand it's not evidence, Your Honour. I am putting on the record for the purposes of appeal to preserve the Prosecution's position that the Trial Chamber permitted the Defence to cross-examine witnesses on prior inconsistent statements made out of court, prior statements, but has not allowed the Prosecution to cross-examine a witness as to a prior inconsistent statement. I would like that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is not correct. You are dealing with Prosecution witness statements that were recorded by investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: These were recorded by -- by lawyers on the other side. They asked questions. They asked the witness questions. The witness answered questions in relation to -- it was only last month -- in relation to issues before the case. And the witness gave different answers in his statement in -- than he gave in evidence yesterday. There are striking differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we are wasting time. You have made your point. It is on record. Please proceed. Yes, Mr. Re, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, your evidence is that only one soldier came with Mr. Tadic. It wasn't two, three, four, five, or more soldiers. That's your evidence, sir, in this court?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the entrance into -- my entrance into the building, first the soldier came, Micic, and then Mr. Tadic. I'm not saying that in the yard there weren't any more soldiers. They went to different entrances into the building to ask people to return the weapons they have, those people who have illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Well, how many soldiers came into the building, apart from Micic, when Micic and Tadic were talking to you? How many other soldiers did you hear going through the building, sir? Because there was more than one, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any other soldier, because I did not go out into the street or into the yard, but I think that there were soldiers who went from one entrance to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you hear going through the -- going through the block of flats when Mr. Tadic was talking to you, sir? How many sets of footsteps did you hear on the stairs going up and down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, how can a witness answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you just hear footsteps, how do you know whose footsteps they are? These are apartment where is the tenants were residing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah, all of them in his flat at the same time, he said, with the door locked downstairs because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. But even then you cannot tell those are footsteps of the soldiers. I will not allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you hear anything outside when you were talking to Mr. Tadic? Did you hear anything that suggested other people were in the building, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tadic, while he was in my building, except for Micic, there was no other soldier at my entrance into the building, in my stairwell. When Mr. Tadic said goodbye to us, I saw them off into the yard and there in the yard I saw two soldiers, and I know who they are. They are soldiers from my building, Dragan -- or rather, Slobodan Antic and Ilija Ilic. They were in uniform. I saw the two of them in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the soldiers who searched the flat of Vera Avdic? Who are they? Who are the soldiers who searched her flat, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the apartment of Vera Avdic, I don't know who entered it, because I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you're aware that some soldiers entered on that day, aren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not some soldiers. They were soldiers who were looking for weapons. Only Micic was at my apartment in my stairwell, and Mr. Tadic. I did not go to the other entrances. The building has eight entrances. I saw Mr. Tadic off to the door, and I went to sit with my neighbours because there was still shooting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said you didn't know who entered Vera Avdic's apartment because you didn't see it. The fact is, you were told or you were aware that some soldiers or a soldier had entered Vera Avdic's apartment on that day looking for weapons, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also a moment ago just said there were soldiers looking for weapons, not some soldiers -- you said, "Well, it's not some soldiers. There were soldiers who were looking for weapons." You said soldiers, more than one. You mean by that, don't you, sir, that more than one soldier came to that apartment block looking for weapons on that day, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you once again that at my entrance into the building and at my stairwell there was only Mr. Tadic and that soldier, Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you said "there were soldiers" looking for weapons, what did you mean by that, sir, if not there were soldiers looking for weapons in the building? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soldiers are the ones I saw when I was seeing off Mr. Tadic. These were soldiers who were in the yard of the building, in the yard of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Looking for weapons, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they were doing, because I did not go to the first or fifth or seventh or third entrance to the building. My entrance to the building is entrance number two, and that's where these two gentleman were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, why did you say there were soldiers looking for weapons if you weren't sure, sir? That's what you said a few moments ago. Why did you say that if you weren't sure?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a soldier walked into my entrance to look for weapons, I assume that the others went to look for the same thing. And that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the first time that you were asked to remember what happened on that date, sir, and write it down? When was the first time you were asked to tell someone about what happened on that day or to write it down? Was it this year, last year?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was it? Let me try to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, don't look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember what year this was when I made this statement. I really can't. Last year a family member of mine died, and I barely remember anything any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you made this statement in February of this year if that assists. Was that the first time that anyone had asked you to remember what happened when Mr. Tadic came to your flat?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't the first time. Other people asked me that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the first time Mr. Lukic asked you or any of the accused -- was that the first time lawyers, or investigators for any of the accused, had asked you to remember about the time Mr. Tadic came to your flat, sir? This year. Don't look that way. Look this way, please.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when they spoke to you, did they ask you what happened on the 18th? Is that what they said to you: What happened on the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they asked me what I stated, and I told you that. I didn't, anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the date. Did they ask you when they spoke to you: What happened on the 18th, Mr. Tubakovic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you had any reason to connect or to associate the 18th with the time that Mr. Tadic came to your flat, that is, being asked 11 years later?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what happened on the 17th, sir? Are you able to tell us now what happened on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us -- I don't want you to tell --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That 17th --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what happened on the 17th? Can you remember what happened on the 17th is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the 19th, sir, the 20th, the 21st, the 22nd, the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you are harassing the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I will not allow this to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not allowed to test his memory. He's given evidence about a specific date. Your Honour is not allowing me to ask him about the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. This type of questioning amounts to harassing the witness. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is the view of the Trial Chamber just go ahead with other questions. Don't harass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand what Your Honour is saying. Could I ask for directions as to how I could ask the witness to test his memory as to other events in the remainder of the week, for example, as to the reliability of his memory as to a certain date? Could Your Honour suggest as to a way I could ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're supposed to cross-examine him on the evidence he has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, his evidence is of a specific date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And you also seek any other evidence that may be supporting your case, but not harassing the witness in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I say to the Court the Prosecutor is trying to test the witness's memory, bearing in mind your decision. But desires of confirming the veracity of this witness. May I say something? I've had long conversations with this witness. Could you please move away a little bit. Could you please move away. I fully agree with my learned friend asking him about the date. Let him ask it and so we shall see how well this witness remembers. I think the Prosecution should really see how good this witness's memory is, but he indeed had a major tragedy in his family. On the other hand, the Prosecution had 40 minutes. Yesterday, today, we've been discussing things. But we've spent almost -- more than an hour on the cross-examination of this witness. I mean, yesterday he testified for half an hour. Then we spent time debating, and now he's been testifying 35 minutes and 40 minutes have been approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I went for 22 minutes yesterday, Your Honour. I've checked it on the transcript. The remainder, the balance at the very end was related to an objection which was overruled and there was about 10 minutes in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The balance was -- for today you're supposed to have 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry? I mis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Today you're supposed to have 35 minutes, because I recorded the time you started your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But because of the interventions, that is why you're being allowed to take a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, the Secretariat for National Defence in which you worked, it was responsible for mobilisation, was it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 25, you refer to a mobilisation of -- I'm sorry, you referred to inviting several hundred Muslims and Croats to attend a meeting at the memorial centre for the purposes of mobilising and reinforcing units. Now, what happened there, sir, was that your organisation, the Secretariat for National Defence, issued mobilisation summonses to hundreds -- to hundreds of Muslim and Croat men who still remained in Bosanski Samac at about that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course at that time, that was in August 1992, the VRS was at war with the HVO, the HV, and the multi-ethnic army of the state of Bosnia, the ABiH, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But from the command, we received the order to summon military constraints of Muslim, that is, Croat ethnicity, to see which one of them would join the Serb army of their own will. Several hundred were summoned. I believe around 450 military conscripts were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, sir, at that time the Serb -- the Serb specials and paramilitaries had been arresting, detaining, beating up hundreds of Croat and Muslim men and detaining them in facilities in Bosanski Samac, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, after we received the order, we summoned military conscripts. I won't go into who did what apart from me. I'm saying what we did. We received an order. We carried it out. We summoned military conscripts. They were waiting for people from the command, that is, from senior officers, to come and talk with them. They didn't come that day. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, please, that's not what I'm asking you. By that stage in Bosanski Samac the Serb specials, paramilitaries, police, had arrested and detained hundreds of Croats and Muslim men over the previous few months and detained them at the SUP, the TO, and the two schools, and were beating and torturing them. That had happened over the previous few months, hadn't it, before August 1992 when you --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were living in Bosanski Samac during the war, weren't you, sir, and working at the Secretariat for National Defence? When you say you don't know, is it that you didn't know then or you can't remember now?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what they were doing then. I repeat, we summoned those men to voluntarily see which ones of them would care to join the Serb army, because before that in the 4th Department [As interpreted] we had the -- in the 4th Detachment we had people of Muslim and Croat and Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. At that stage in August 1992, Bosanski Samac municipality was under Serb military rule, wasn't it? The VRS, the paramilitaries, the police, and the Crisis Staff had imposed military control over Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course there was no reason and in those circumstances with Serb military control you wouldn't think that Muslims or Croats would want to join an army that was fighting the HVO or the HV or the ABiH, would you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they had in mind. We summoned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, when -- when these people didn't answer their summonses, they swam across the river, didn't they, to get away from Serb military rule and the threat of imprisonment for not obeying the summonses? Didn't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military conscripts or Muslims, that is, Croat ethnicity, responded to the summonses, responded to it. But they were not admitted into the army because nobody from the army came to take them on, apart from the 30 men who volunteered to join the army, and they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, if I misled you slightly. They -- what I suggest is they responded to the summonses and -- and as a result of being told that if they didn't join the army they would be imprisoned, they swam across the river to get away from Serb military rule. That's what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when they swam across the river, sir, their wives and children who were left behind were isolated and taken to Zasavica by the Serb military and civilian authorities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that is not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, how was it, sir? When they swam across the river, what did happen to their wives and children, sir, in August 1992? What happened to their wives and children?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military conscripts of the Muslim, that is, Croat ethnicity, whom we had summoned and who responded to the summons, came to the place where they were summoned to report to, were waiting, and we waited with them for somebody from the army to come and talk to them. But nobody from the army turned up. Nevertheless, those 30 or so soldiers said that they would join the Army of Republika Srpska. After that I do not know who swam and went into the Sava, as said. However, their families, wives, and children were not detained because of that. They were isolated because the HVO troops and those other Croat troops had attacked Serb troops in the village, in Novo Selo, and on that occasion several Serb soldiers were killed, and that was why women and children were isolated, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Jelena Kapetanovic, who lived in your apartment block, was taken to Zasavica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you should be winding up. Your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask him one area, that's the labour system in which he was working, relating to paragraph 9 of his -- of his statement, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. But your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has had some difficulties with the places on the -- with the time limits which have been imposed upon the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not going to discuss that. The Trial Chamber did say the opportunity for cross-examination on the similar issues has already been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, in relation -- in your statement you referred to -- you referred to work obligation being within the framework of the Secretariat for National Defence. Now, the way that worked was that civil protection needed labour; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work obligation was the responsibility of the Secretariat for People's Defence outside the building of the Secretariat, and this was done by two employees of the Secretariat for People's Defence. And they replenished the civil defence for those structures which expressed the need for labour. What they did, where did they go, I didn't follow them. And when it comes to Jelena Kapetanovic or former Stanisic, all that she said, that woman, was not telling the truth. I can swear on the life of all that I hold dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, sir, about the labour obligation and your work in the Secretariat for National Defence. You said you were responsible for raising military conscripts for the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Were you or your section also responsible for coordination of civil -- coordination of labour which the military required in its work, either on the front lines or behind the lines?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the labour which you obtained to assist the military with their work on the front lines or behind the lines, the civilian labour, did you obtain that through coordination or speaking to civil protection? Where did you get the labour from, to assist the military -- the civilian labour to assist the military with their work on the front lines or behind the lines?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the civil work obligation was prescribed by law. And those who were to be assigned were kept on their record at the Secretariat, and that record also said where they should go to work and what they should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want to know is where -- if you received a request from, say, the 2nd Posavina Brigade for some civilian labour, where did you, sir, obtain the labour from? Who gave you the list? You gave you the names? Who physically arranged for these people to go and help the military either at the front or behind the lines?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our secretariat had the roster of the military conscripts and other citizens who were supposed to and were under work obligation. And pursuant to an order from the command, my two colleagues, who were engaged in that particular aspect of work, we issued them orders and they sent people where they had been asked to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just clarify who the command was? This is an important part for both cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re. This is going on for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the Trial Chamber clear on the links between the two based on that witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You cannot ask that question, Mr. Re. We've got so much evidence on this question of where the labour -- who organised the labour, for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you sit down. Yes, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, we won't keep you much longer here, but we need to shed more light on some of the answers that you gave the Prosecution. When you were asked about telephones today, you mentioned - and that is on page 4, that is how I recorded today - that when telephone lines were re-established, that you talked with Mehmed Halibegovic [As interpreted] and you also mentioned another last name and said that you also talked to that man.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Halilovic and Avdibegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you just tell the Chamber what is the ethnic origin of those two men that you talked with over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their ethnicity is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned when the Prosecutor asked you today about the arrival of Tadic and Micic to your building, and you said that later on when you came out in front of your yard that you also saw your neighbours Slobodan Antic and Ilija Ilic. That is how I recorded it. Were they also wearing military uniforms and were they also your neighbours or your co-townsmen? That is what I'm asking you, witness.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether they were members of the 4th Detachment? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing uniforms and they were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you pause in question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm about to finish my last witness, and it seems that I haven't learned over this past year and a half to examine correctly. My apologies to the interpreters once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, do you recall the day when Tadic came, when they searched for weapons, whether that day, whether in the course of that day whether anyone else came again to look for weapons in your building?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I have only one more question. The Prosecutor asked you about that, about that rally in front of the memorial centre, and you mentioned in paragraph 25 of your written statement. Do you remember who was there with you present in front of the Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There was the head of a department, Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let us clear up another question which you were asked by the Prosecution in relation to those persons and those summonses. Did any of you who was at that rally, I mean both you, Bozo Ninkovic, or somebody else, if there was somebody else representing the authorities of the Serb municipality, that is, the Secretariat for People's Defence, did any one of you say on that occasion to those hundreds of Muslims and Croats that they had to respond to the summonses or else they'd be detained?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. Had we wanted to detain them, we could have done that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you say that something else unpleasant could happen to them if they didn't respond to the summons?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... there's a document in evidence, D37 -- sorry, 34/3, which is what I was referring to, and I think Mr. Lukic knows that. It was a document tendered by, I think, Mr. Lukic, of a summons. That's what I was questioning the witness about, the summons. And it lists exactly the penalties, and we've heard evidence as to what happened -- what they were told would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But I thought that -- if any Defence witness is contradicting other Defence witnesses, that would be ammunition for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was particularly interested to learn about the question, that is what I asked, whether this was mentioned at that rally, whether at that particular rally anyone said that somebody might be arrested or that something bad may happen to him, that he could come to harm if he failed to respond to the summons.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tubakovic, I have a few questions which I would like to pose to you based on what you said yesterday and a few things this morning. The first question concerns something with respect to yesterday. And for the sake of counsel, I'll refer you to the page I'm thinking of on the LiveNote of yesterday, page 83, line 10. Mr. Tubakovic, you mentioned yesterday that a combat vehicle - I believe it's called an ACV - was going along the other side of the street from your building on Edvarda Kardelja, I apologise for my pronunciation, number 62. And it said in the transcript - at least, this is the English translation - that the barrel, presumably one of the barrels on this vehicle, was pointing at your building. And I'd like to ask you: If you know, why was this barrel of this combat vehicle, ACV, pointing towards your building? It seems rather a threatening gesture. If you have no knowledge, just say that. But I'm just interested to know your reaction.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ACV which was going down the Edvard Kardelj Street and turned right to Sokolusa Street, that is, to the south of our building, and it had come precisely because there'd been gunfire opened from the building. Yesterday I said about referring to this [redacted], that there was a general opinion and that people knew that [redacted] had a sniper in his house, and he used that weapon. However, yesterday when I said that Mr. Tadic invited him to turn down his weapon, he said that he didn't have one, and at that time he didn't have it at home. But later on it turned out that this sniper was being brought by his sister-in-law from another street, that she would have it under her kitchen coveralls and that they would open fire and that woman could take back that weapon back to her apartment, and that is why this vehicle came and of course the barrel was pointed and we watched it, all of us, all the tenants were watching it from my flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question -- sorry. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise that I'm interfering, but perhaps because of the names, perhaps the transcript should be redacted where the names that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So Mr. Tubakovic, thank you for that clarification. My second question concerns your apartment building. I wonder whether you can remember whether the soldier who came on the 18th or Mr. Tadic or any other soldier who came later on ever told you or the other tenants, if you know, whether you had to keep your apartment doors unlocked at all times.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I affirm it most emphatically that nobody ever said anything with regard to the doors, whether the flats should be locked up or unlocked. Before the combat operations started, the door was already broken because it was made of glass and then we organised ourselves and we all made tin plate doors in the -- as our front doors, and those doors were locked up at 10.00 every night. And when combat operations started, this Micic, who came on the 18th, I opened the door for him personally and he was very -- he reacted very noisily, "Why this door locked?" And I told him, "Keep your voice down. I opened it." And Mr. Tadic came after him and said, "What's this about, neighbour?" And I said, "Well, this one is making too much noise." Nobody had ordered anyone or said that door should be locked or unlocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. But that clearly is the front door to the series of apartments that you had one of. I'm not just thinking of the front door down below, or at the ground level, but I'm thinking of the individual apartment doors, for example, your apartment, that of Jelena Kapetanovic, and others, the individual apartment doors is what I'm thinking of. Was anybody told, that you're aware of, including yourself, that you had to not lock your door day or night, of your own individual apartment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much. Just moving on, because I do have two or three other short questions. From what you said yesterday it's clear that apart from yourself, in this whole number 62 building with its various entrance ways, that Mr. Tadic - Miroslav Tadic, that is - and Dr. Blagoje Simic also had apartments in this same complex. No? I see Mr. Lukic is standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for suggesting, but he said Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic had it in that building, while Tadic lives next to his cafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, Mr. Tadic. I realise from the photographs. I have a visualisation of your premises. Yes. Mr. Zaric and Dr. Blagoje Simic also lived in the same apartment complex. My question, Mr. Tubakovic, is: During the period before April 17th, 1992 and subsequent to that, did you ever see Mr. Tadic, Mr. Zaric, and Dr. Blagoje Simic going together to visit in Mr. Zaric's apartment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, going just on to this morning. You said - and for sake of counsel, this is LiveNote page 7, line 25 - the question to you was whether there were only two persons came to your apartment, I think it was the 18th, and that was the soldier, Micic, and Mr. Tadic. And your answer on line 25 was, "Yes. At that time, when they came, yes." Now, it strikes me just from that answer where you say "at that time" that there must have been other times as well. Were there any other occasions when soldiers or Mr. Tadic or both together visited your section of number 62?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the Sule Micic and Mr. Tadic left, no one from the Army of Republika Srpska came to visit. The members of the internal affairs police did come because for a long period it was thought that from that very entranceway, from that floor, the shots were fired, and the police came to look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just my last and very brief question is concerning - and again, for counsels' sake, this is page 21, lines 24 and following - and this is concerning the question by the Prosecutor, Mr. Re, with respect to persons swimming over the River Sava and the relatives being placed in isolation in Zasavica. Now, obviously, Mr. Tubakovic, you know, from your statement and so on, you know Mrs. Jelena Kapetanovic very well. And my question to you is, based on what you said to Mr. Re earlier on this morning, I just wonder, being that you know her so well, why or do you know why she was sent to -- first of all, to Crkvina, and then to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why she was sent there, but I do know her very, very well, this woman, and I know that whatever she said in her statement, that 99 per cent of that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, my follow-up question is: Based on your answer this morning, and now you've repeated it, where you say this morning at lines 13 to 15 on page 23, that "All she said, that woman, was not telling the truth." I'm just wondering how you know what she said in her statement and how you know that she was not telling the truth before this Tribunal. I mean, are you aware of the testimony that she provided to us here?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how she testified here, but I know that Mr. Lukic told me approximately what she had said, and that is why I'm here, to deny that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And last but not least: Do you know whether Mrs. Kapetanovic's then-boyfriend, now husband, swam across the River Sava, was one of those 30-odd men who took off to Croatia and swam across the Sava?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I know this boy -- well, he was born in 1969. His name is Ersef. As far as I remember, it is quite possible that he left as well. I know that his uncle, his father's brother, and his two children went across Sava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, I'll catch the opportunity and hook up on a question posed to you by Judge Williams and also touched upon by Mr. Lukic and concerning the search for weapons, about which you have told us repeatedly that it happened in the way that a soldier by the name of Micic came to your entrance, followed after a while by Mr. Tadic. And at that time almost all of the inhabitants in your entrance were gathered in your apartment. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And there's been some indications or, let's say, questions pointing to the possibility that there was perhaps further searches for weapons. And now I am asking you: Do you know a person by the name Naser Sejdic, also nicknamed Sahara [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Cakara, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Cakara. Yes. Naser Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic, also known as Cakara, yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Close to those events, around the 17th and the days after that, did he perhaps ever enter your entrance together with other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic was a policeman and not a soldier. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. But did you ever see him close to those days together -- as a policeman, but together with other persons in military uniforms, camouflage uniforms, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And nobody told you about a visit by him and a group of five other uniformed men in your entrance?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Tadic and Micic left the building, I cannot remember whether it was the same day or the day after that Naser Sejdic, the policeman, and another man who I know came. They called him -- what's his name? Let me remember. Ibrahim is his first name. His nickname -- he has a very nice nickname, but I can't remember. They came to the building only to go into Porobic's apartment. His nickname is Caba, Ibrahim's nickname. And that was on the 19th. Yes, that's right. And he dropped by my apartment because the other, Ibrahim, also nobody as Caba, he married a daughter of one of my relatives, so I called him as my son-in-law, so I asked him, "Well, what happened? Where were you?" And he said, "Well, we were up there at Cuka's and they told us again that somebody was opening fire there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But they weren't systematically searching for weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were following orders, because the -- when the army passed on the 18th, nobody came afterwards to search for weapons -- well, at least, nobody came to my building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And they were all only two persons, not a group of five or six?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was Naser and Ibrahim was in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic, for giving evidence. We are now finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the next witness is brought in, as a result of this witness's evidence, the Prosecution -- I appreciate Your Honours will be against me -- wishes to move into evidence those portions of the 92 bis statement D184/3. I'm doing this formally for the purposes of the record, D184/3. I anticipate Your Honours will be against me, but I -- I offer the -- I give the following offer of proof in relation to the matters which the Prosecution would have cross-examined the witness on and his anticipated answers so that it's on the record. I would have cross-examined the witness as to his statement in paragraph 11 that: "Soldiers entered the building before Miroslav Tadic and were seeking weapons. And apart from the flat of Vera Avdic, who told them she did not have any weapon, did enter any of the other flats from the tenants that I could see." I would have cross-examined him on his statement that, "I did not see whether Miroslav Tadic was armed on that occasion," and in consistency with his evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, what are you doing? You are still going back to the paragraphs that were struck off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an offer of proof. For the record for appellant proceedings, I am putting on the record what we would have cross-examined the witness on. So it's on the record. It's not part of the evidence. And finally that he said: "Soldiers who had come into the block heard this too and were searching the flats in the build." I would have -- let me just finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I oppose. He is dictating into the record everything that the Honourable Judges actually struck out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not. This is an offer of proof. You're professional Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just my submission. I was just trying to make a legal submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I've finished my legal submission. It's an offer of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? Your Honours, if I may address you, based on this request by the Prosecution, I would ask the Court that the whole part explaining the facts underlying the request be struck from the transcript because in this way there is an attempt to put to the Chamber something that has not been the basis of the case. We know that when the witness was in the courtroom I was able to clarify certain facts, but the Chamber forbade me to actually put questions on some issues. Now, if the Prosecution has some sort of a legal problem, then this is how it should be formulated and not backed by facts. I will remind the Chamber when we were talking about the telephone interview with Mr. Tadic, the Prosecution first gave you the interview and then gave the legal request. I think they should first present a legal request instead of presenting facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to explain an offer of proof is used in a number of different jurisdictions around the world. I'm not sure if it's used in all of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber rules that there is a misunderstanding on the procedure of Rule 92 bis. As far as the Chamber is concerned, paragraphs that are struck off in any of the statements submitted are not supposed to be resurrected by being referred to at all. There are situations where some paragraphs have been struck off and the Trial Chamber has decided that the witness will not come, either for examination-in-chief or for cross-examination. And this ought to be the same regarding the statements where witnesses have been allowed to come either for viva voce or for cross-examination. The application by the Prosecution is misconceived and is, therefore, denied. Yes. We have another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I have copies of the redacted statement of this witness, so I would kindly ask the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Could you just for the record state your name.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Stanko Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All the events that you explained in your statement have entered the record, apart from paragraphs 11 and 12, so I won't be asking you specifically about that but I will ask you about the part of your testimony related to your stay in Cafe AS in the night -- on the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So I kindly ask you, when I will be asking you questions, to be focussed on these issues so that I don't have to put to you leading questions.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you when you hear my question to pause for a few seconds and then give your answer. This is due to the interpreters, so that there would be no overlapping.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, you were in the Cafe AS in the night of the 16th of April. Could you briefly tell us when you arrived, how long you stayed there, and could you simply tell us everything that happened that night.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in the evening, around 8.00. That is the place where we mostly gathered, played cards, shot pool. Somebody would watch the TV, if there was a football match on. There was this group of people that I met on a daily basis and socialised with. We used to stay very long in the night. And then that particular evening there was maybe ten of us Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. There was Avdo; there was Nenad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It isn't necessary for you -- you should go back to the period when you heard shots.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: All right. That was around 2.30 when we heard an explosion, first one explosion then a second one as well. We were frightened a bit, and those whose houses were nearby went home and we stayed there. We were friends with Mr. Tadic's son and Mr. Tadic asked us, since my house is a kilometre and a half away from the cafe, he offered us to stay overnight so that nothing would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, who stayed, apart from you, in that -- on that evening in Mr. Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Nenad Tomasovic stayed with me. He was a friend of mine who came from Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who else was there? Was there Miroslav Tadic as well?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Miroslav Tadic, his son, and Mrs. Mirjana, Miroslav Tadic wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay at the cafe, or did you at a certain point go into the house?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, first we stayed in the cafe. Mr. Miroslav Tadic tried to reach someone on the phone to see what was going on; however, the phone was down, the communications were done. And then he told us to go upstairs where his son -- his son's room was. And Nenad and I were in one room and his son was in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue at 11.00 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, before the break, you said that after Miroslav Tadic locked his cafe, you went upstairs and you indeed went upstairs. You were near the rooms where Mr. Tadic's son lived. Tell me, Mr. Bojic, what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: And when the shooting abated, we went to bed and fell asleep. In the morning, I work up. I went out to the terrace in my underwear to stretch out a bit, but somebody fired a bullet and the bullet went right by me, and I fled into the room. In the room, we got ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, we'll get to that. But I just wanted to ask you: Do you remember approximately what time that was when you got up and when you went out onto the terrace?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It was about 8.00, 7.30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see where this first shot came from, the shot that went at you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: And then we got ready, all three of us. We went out onto the terrace, and in the distance we saw some soldiers and we saw that they were wearing some kind of camouflage uniforms, and we recognised some of the young men who were from the neighbouring villages. They first got into the health centre, and they drove out the doctors and nurses, lined them up by the fence of the soccer -- football club called Borac, they frisked them, and then they returned them. When they got about 50 or 60 or 70 metres away from us, then they opened fire against us. These were bursts of gunfire, and we lay down immediately. Then Mr. Miroslav Tadic ran up to us. He was carrying a white sheet, and he also took a big stick and then he made a make-shift white flag, and that is how they stopped shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. We'll get to that. In relation to the first time you appeared on the terrace, when you were shot at, when did this other event occur, this second round of shooting that you just described?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It was around 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please proceed. Where did these soldiers go after that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: They went down the street by Miroslav Tadic's. One of them went towards the -- one group of them went towards the embankment and another group went towards the post office. Afterwards we went downstairs into the cafe, and then I went back to my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bojic, the health centre and Miroslav Tadic's house, are there any buildings between the two that block the view, or is there just an empty area between the two?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: There's just an empty area between the two. Until the present day, there have been no buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: These people you've just described, you said that they were multicoloured. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I meant they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these people later?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, we did. All the time, for part of the war. Later on they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: These people were from Serbia. At least, that's what they said, or that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was Miroslav Tadic's house damaged visibly then?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They hit the bricks, the glass, also the wood panelling behind us, then on the terrace there were parts of concrete that were ripped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately how many gunshots were fired this second time to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: About 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, my name is Di Fazio. I have a few questions for you. Hopefully we'll be very brief. You were a member of the 4th Detachment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The purpose of the 4th Detachment, you agree, was to defend the town from outside attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. The second objective of the 4th Detachment was to prevent inter-ethnic strife?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And to protect the people and the property of Bosanski Samac and that area?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the months leading up to April 16, the 4th Detachment armed itself - in other words, it distributed arms to its members.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, that the purpose of arming individual members of the 4th Detachment was so that they could carry out those objects -- objectives, I should say, of defending the town from outside attack, preventing inter-ethnic strife, and protecting people of all ethnicity and protecting their property. That's the reason why they were given guns.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the members of the 4th Detachment who were given guns kept those weapons at home.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you had your own 4th Detachment weapon issued to you which you kept at your home.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And do you know if Mr. Tadic kept his own 4th Detachment weapon at the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think he did at the cafe. Perhaps somewhere in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The house is downstairs, isn't it? It's part of the Cafe AS complex or building.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have your own personal weapon? I mean, one not given to you by the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were required to attend training sessions in the period of time leading up to April 16, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, this was just some training in marksmanship, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Thank you. And the 4th Detachment was divided up into structure -- into various structures, companies, and further units?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And clearly, what you've testified just now, regarding the objects and purposes of the 4th Detachment and preparations it made to carry out its mission, was known to all 4th Detachment members?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sorry. I didn't -- I was waiting for your answer. I didn't realise you hadn't heard me. All the -- the evidence you've just given regarding the purposes, the objectives of the 4th Detachment, and all the preparations it made, training, organising itself into various units, and so on, all of that was clearly known and understood by every member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell the Chamber what your orders were in the event of an attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in the event of an attack, I received call-up papers to report at my platoon and then we should go to the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you're describing what in fact happened, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll get to that later. I'm not asking you about what in fact happened. I want to know what your orders were in the event of an attack on Bosanski Samac. In the event of an attack on the personal property of the residents of Bosanski Samac or in the event of inter-ethnic strife or in the event that the town was attacked from outside, what were your orders? What were you to do if that event happened?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know? I don't really remember these orders very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were no orders for just such a contingency?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the town was supposed to be defended. That meant from an external enemy. Because in the detachment, there were people of all ethnic backgrounds. We did not expect a war from the inside. Because people were talking about the fact that there would be an attack from Croatia, Slavonia, from Prud, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Just tell the Judges, tell the Trial Chamber what the 4th Detachment was expected to do if the Croatians came streaming across the bridge armed to the teeth and shooting guns.
