What was the 4th Detachment to do? Please tell the Chamber. Because that was your purpose, you see, and that's what I want to know. What were your orders to do in the event of an attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: To protect the town and the people in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I know that. I understand that. I'm not quarreling with you, and I understand that perfectly well. I know what your objectives were, and you've already told us what the objectives were. What I want to know is what were the orders for you to do in the event that shooting started, bombing started, an attack on the town started? Did you have any orders for that contingency?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you just a while ago that we were supposed to go to the embankment and protect the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So that was a -- perhaps I misunderstood you. That was an order that was issued to you long before the 16th and 17th. It was an order that was issued to you to go to the embankment well before the 16th and 17th.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did not receive this order. The commanding officers got that order. I was an ordinary soldier. When they convened us, then they sent us to the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, and I'm grateful for you to have told us and informed us of that. Can we just move away, though, from what you actually did. And just for the last time, if we can, go back to the period of time, weeks and days, before the 16th. Okay? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in those weeks and days, the object of the 4th Detachment was to protect the town against attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Not probably. You've told us that that was one of the objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: But I'm not the one who was actually deciding. I was just a soldier. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I understand perfectly well. You weren't a commander, were you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So we're talking about the period of time before the night of the 16th and 17th. Now, the purpose of the 4th Detachment was to protect the town against attack. Attacks are sudden events. What were your instructions or standing orders in the event of such an attack? For example, hordes of Croatians crossing across the river. What -- did you have any standing orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the witness has already answered this question and that he does not recall any such orders. He's an ordinary soldier. He already said that when giving evidence in response to the Prosecutor's question that he did not recall such orders before the 16th of April, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: May I adopt Mr. Krgovic's suggestion and language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There were no orders, were there, for you common soldiers in the 4th Detachment relating to a surprise attack, were there? You didn't know what to do, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody would have probably informed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll leave that topic. On the morning of the 17th, on the morning of the 17th, did you see a combat vehicle with a group of masked soldiers with automatic rifles escorting it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw a small TAM truck with a machine-gun on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just tell the Chamber what a TAM truck is exactly, please.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It's a little truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. But is it an armoured truck? Does it have special military features?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "military features"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: On top of this small truck there was a heavy calibre powerful submachine-gun; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the truck armoured? Did it have extra armour?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It's a truck. In our part of the world, it was mostly used for smuggling peppers. That's the kind of small truck it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it an army-issue truck?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I think so [As interpreted]. Well, maybe it was actually. I have no idea who it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The answer was "I don't think so," not "I think so." This is what we heard from the witness, "I don't think so." This was the answer on page 49, line 13. First he said "I don't think so. Well, maybe it was." MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Your answer was when I asked you if it was an army-issue truck, your answer was "I don't think so. Maybe it was actually. I have no idea who it belonged to." Is that correct? Was that your answer? Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did the truck have any markings on it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No special ones. I don't remember. I don't think it had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This truck that you saw was taking over the town, wasn't it, and it was surrounded by armed masked, camouflaged men? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: They didn't have any kind of masks. Well, they weren't taking over. I think they were going around, disarming these paramilitary Muslims, as we call them, those who had received weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's on the morning of the 17th; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, it was the morning of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They did that throughout the day and on the 18th as well?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so, because I was not in town on that day, on the 18th. I was there just for a little while. I was at the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So they were doing the same thing that the 4th Detachment was doing, disarming the population?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the 4th Detachment was doing less of the disarming. It was at the embankment. And I don't know what other units were doing. I know about my own platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that the 4th Detachment participated in the seizure or the taking or the collection of weapons from the population of the town on the 17th and 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: This was probably done by another part that was in town, but I was at the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. You know, don't you, that another part of the 4th Detachment was engaged in taking or seizing or collecting weapons from the population of the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I've already said to you a short while ago that I was at the embankment and what these others did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you testifying to the Chamber that you don't know of any order issued to the 4th Detachment on the 17th of April, 1992 that weapons were to be collected from the population? You don't know of any such order, never heard of it, never reported to you, never informed of it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I heard that these weapons were being collected and that this was probably being done by the many-coloured ones, and we were done there at the embankment and we were not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So the result is that you don't know of any order issued to the 4th Detachment to collect weapons. You never heard it. You're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the detachment had several companies and platoons. My platoon did not receive these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you can tell us that the Sareni, the camouflaged ones, the ones with the machine-gun and truck, were going around collecting weapons. Can you answer my question? I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, somebody told us down there at the embankment that they were also collecting these weapons in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Just so that we can get this done a bit faster, witness, if you answer my questions -- you have to answer my questions so it's recorded and then a transcript is made. So there's no point not saying anything. You have to answer my questions, say something at least, so it's recorded. Okay?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, I believe I found out what was the problem. At the end f every question maybe he should say is that right, is that correct, or something like that, otherwise, the witness is waiting for the end of your question and he just doesn't receive it. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. I'll do that. I'm sorry if that's what's been happening. I'll make it clearer that I'm in fact asking you questions. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the early -- in the morning of the 17th, you'd heard explosions in the town, the sound of gunfire, and Mr. Tadic's cafe had been fired upon, bullets narrowly missing you. You and Mr. Tadic and the others in the house, I assume, were all desperate to know exactly what was going on; is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And it was apparent to you, as a member of the 4th Detachment, that the town was under attack. That's a fair comment as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On what? What --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps had the Croats come in, then perhaps yes. But they were not killing anyone, so it wasn't. What kind of an attack on the town was it? Nobody got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Explosions in the town, men walking around with armed automatic weapons shooting at houses. You say that the town is not under attack? Are you serious?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: There were no casualties in the town. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: None that you knew of at that time. But it was -- casualties or otherwise, it was overpoweringly obvious to you, wasn't it, overwhelmingly obvious to you that the town was under an attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we were three of us there under attack on the terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. But you could hear fighting in the distance, couldn't you, shooting around the town and explosions?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no gunfire or explosions in daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Right. So the town didn't have -- you didn't see anything that gave you the impression that the town was under attack.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Why, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did Mr. Tadic -- sorry, let me withdraw that. Did you and Mr. Tadic and the other people who were there in the Cafe AS on this morning of the 17th, 1992 discuss the question of whether or not the town was under attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Now, that Mr. Tadic was down there, a floor below with his mistress [As interpreted], and we were sitting upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Did you have an opportunity at all on that morning to -- to share any views with any other people in the house as to whether or not the town was under attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... with who?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Tadic's son and Nenad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you satisfy yourselves that the town was not under attack?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: We were waiting for information. We were waiting to hear from the command to tell us what to do, but nobody did, and I went home, and it was only when I got there I found the summons to report to the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunate interpretation could cause a lot of problems for Mr. Tadic. So I would like to correct it. It's on page 53, line 19. He said he was a floor below with his madam. This is what he said. Meaning his wife. And he says with his mistress, and this is just not what the witness said. MR. DI FAZIO: I didn't think that was a likely meaning of the witness, if Your Honours please, and I accept what Mr. Lazarevic says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That can -- yes. That can be clarified by the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Earlier you told us where Mr. Tadic was. He was downstairs with his wife; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: At the mezzanine, because there is the coffee bar on the ground floor and there are two floors above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. With his wife, his wife, the woman he is married to?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, following the -- your conclusion that the town was not under attack, it was clear that there was some hooligans at work because they had shot at the house of Mr. Tadic. Did you go and report it to the police or try to report it to the police?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I've told you that I had gone home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to that issue, then. You went home and you received a message to report to the 4th Detachment; am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Received the call-up summons to report to the call-up meeting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What call-up meeting point?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Slijvak, the plum orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was this a standing instruction, some order that you had that existed prior to the 16th and 17th that there was a meeting point called the plum orchard?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you were only told to meet at the plum orchard on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And about what time did you receive your orders to go to the meeting point at the plum orchard?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the afternoon, around 2.00 or maybe 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So you got your gun, your automatic weapon, and you walked out of your house with your automatic weapon, and you went down to the plum orchard; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And when you got to the plum orchard, you saw assembled other members of the 4th Detachment also carrying their automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were they in uniform or some of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, some were, but most of them were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about how many men gathered in the plum orchard?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we were about 20 at that time, about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Chamber if you had or experienced any difficulties in walking with an automatic rifle from your house to the plum orchard. You didn't come across, for example, the likes of Lugar, or Laki, or any of the other Serbian paramilitaries by any chance?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because my house is at the very end of the town and this plum orchard, where we were to meet, is about halfway to the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. And in that time, you had no difficulties in -- with any paramilitaries that you -- that you're aware of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber if any of the other 20 or so men who had arrived armed at the plum orchard experienced any difficulties with the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose had they had any, they wouldn't have come. Because this is mostly my neighbourhood, my area, one house next to the other almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You know, don't you, that a number of paramilitaries, consisting of local people and also some men from Serbia, came into the town, basically took over the town on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, and that a Serb Crisis Staff suddenly appeared and took control of the town? That all happened on the night of the 16th, 17th, and in the days following. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You're not aware of there being a Serb Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac in the days following the 16th and -- sorry, the 17th and 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I heard about it, but much later on. I didn't know. And there wasn't -- I didn't really want to know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell me, have you ever heard of something called the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac? Have you ever heard of such a body?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you hear about that around April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was towards the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know that the Serb police under a man named Stevan Todorovic took control of the police station and that paramilitaries took control of vital points and facilities around the town on the night of the 16th and 17th? Have you ever heard of that happening?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that they had been taken over, I mean, these vital facilities taken that evening, 16th and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return now to the issue of the meeting at the plum orchard. You see, the town was crawling, wasn't it, with paramilitaries, these people who had taken over the town? They were driving around in their armoured truck with machine-guns on it; they were all armed to the teeth; a good number of them were men you didn't know or recognise or weren't known or recognisable to other members of the 4th Detachment because they came from Serbia. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any paramilitaries at all on the 17th? Did you see any of them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Later on, when I went home and I returned, and I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it was the next day when I saw it, but not that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So they -- you saw armed paramilitaries on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And when you saw them, you were armed.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what your instructions were in the event of an encounter between members of the 4th Detachment and armed Serbian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why didn't you shoot them? I mean, these are armed men, and you're protecting the town, you don't know who they are, you've got no instructions, they're not recognisable as members of the 4th Detachment. Why not do something about them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Would you fire and then get killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fortunately, I wasn't there. But you were, and you were a member of the 4th Detachment. So I'm asking you: Your job was to protect the town. Here are armed men. You don't have any instructions. Why didn't you take action?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Because I wasn't given orders from the command, that is, from my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did anyone in the command at any time tell you who these men were and how you were supposed to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in the command, and I don't know what they were saying there, talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it that no, you never received any instructions from your commanders on how to deal with these paramilitaries, what to do in the event of an encounter.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's because you were cooperating with them in the takeover of the town, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's move to another topic. Now, you had to wear white ribbons, I think, for a few days. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that very soon -- well, let me withdraw that. Was that on the 17th that you were issued with that order?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, in the afternoon, when we got together there, at that place. That's when they told us to put on those white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. The -- all the members of the 4th Detachment were locals, weren't they? They were all from --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In fact, am I right that they were all in fact from the town itself, not actually the municipality but all from the town itself of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, they were also from around the town, from villages. They were not all from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And one thing is for sure: All of you recognised each other and knew each other well; right?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You all knew each other well. You had worked together, trained together. It was required that you knew who was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Why, we couldn't all know everything about everybody who was there. Everybody knew more or less his platoon, his company, and those at the other end of the town knew their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did anyone give you any explanation as to the purpose of your wearing white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was kind of identification. But everybody wore those ribbons, the civilian population, Serbs, and Croats, and Muslims, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone give you the explanation for members of the 4th Detachment being ordered to wear white ribbons on the 17th in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Nobody. Just "Put those white ribbons on."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Up until that point in its operations, the 4th Detachment had not worn white ribbons, had it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: I apologise, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Up until that time, up until the afternoon of the 17th, the 4th Detachment hadn't worn white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It had carried out its business, its training exercises, its patrols at night --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: There were no patrols or training except for these firing exercises in Potocari, which is a village above Brcko. That's where we were practicing firing. But that was all the training that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Didn't the 4th Detachment have reconnaissance squads, patrols at night?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps yes, but I don't know. I was in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did that mean "perhaps yes, but I don't know"? Tell us. If you know something, tell us clearly. If you don't know something, tell us clearly. But --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Like this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I worked for Uniglas and I worked on three shifts, so that I had those obligations for the company, so I said those people who had less obligations, perhaps they used it, perhaps they patrolled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. Before the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, did the 4th Detachment conduct patrols in and around the town of Bosanski Samac? If you know they did, tell us. If you don't know, tell us that you don't know. Okay? But just be clear about your answer, if you could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Now, as far as the white ribbons are concerned, before the 16th and 17th the 4th Detachment never wore them, did it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The purpose of the white ribbons on the 17th of April, 1992 was to make the 4th Detachment recognisable to these paramilitaries who had taken control of the town. That was its purpose, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the civilians had those ribbons and cars had them on their aerials. Everybody had those white ribbons. The town population by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So one thing you are sure about is that you got an order to go off down to the Bosna and the Sava, or the Sava, and set up a position on the embankment. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: There you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. And how long were you there in your position on the river bank?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was -- what do I know? A couple of days? Changing, somebody comes, you go back home, then you return and they stay behind, and that's how we took shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And -- excuse me, did the shifts sometimes occur at night so that you might be finishing one shift on the bank, another company coming in to take over, and you going -- walking home at night to go home?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No, never at night. That was in the beginning. On a voluntary basis largely, some good terms with him and then he takes over. It wasn't really well organised. There were no official shifts or nothing, but where it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the result is that there were armed 4th Detachment members walking around at night going to and fro their positions on the embankment.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Not by night. The daytime. At night-time nobody took shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The positions on the embankment, that required you to dig in, to form emplacements for heavy machine-guns and also to provide cover for the soldiers, members of the 4th Detachment; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning we didn't even dig in. It was only a few days later. We just lied about on the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So just lay about on the embankment. But in any event, after lying about for a few days, you actually did dig in some positions.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Later on, later on, seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I take it from the fact that you just lay about on the embankment that you weren't too worried about an attack coming from Croatia or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we were not wise to all that war. We didn't know what one should do, because we had an attack precisely from that side on the 17th -- no, I think on the 18th, afternoon, from the direction of Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Were you involved in that particular action?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean was I involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That attack from Prud on the 18th, were you involved in that attack, defending the town, I mean?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did that lead you to dig in?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, we started digging in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Was equipment used for that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we used picks and shovels. Later on they made those concrete bunkers for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have a little -- are you aware of a little tractor being used, some sort of small earth-moving equipment, a piece of earth-moving equipment being used to dig the trenches?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I guess there was, because I told you, I'm not -- you're there for a while, then you go, then you're at home. Nobody forced you to be there on the embankment non-stop. At times you just get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Bojic, I'll leave you alone on topics if you don't know something about it, but I just don't know from your answers whether you know something or whether you don't know. Let me ask again. You asked -- I asked you if there was a little tractor or a small piece of earth-moving equipment being used to dig the trenches. You replied as part of your answer, "I don't remember. I guess there was." Now, do you --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's why I'm saying this. Because from time to time, I'd take to my heels and then I'm not there for a couple of days, I'm staying with my girlfriend. So I mean, there was this, you know. Everybody is over there and you're over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough. So was earth-moving equipment used to dig in on the embankments while you were there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: While I was there, it wasn't used. Mostly the trenches were already dug out. I didn't dig them out, anyway, because I'm lazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you for that. Did you see any Muslims or Croats digging trenches that were to be used by the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, only those who were members of the 4th Detachment were digging, Croats, Muslims, and Serb, because they were digging them out for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At any time that you were in Bosanski Samac in April of 1992, did you see Croats or Muslims who were not members of the 4th Detachment digging trenches, trenches that were used by the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many sons does Mr. Tadic have?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I know only of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of his being involved, the son, that is, in some fracas or incident in the Cafe AS in early 1993 in which a man was hurt?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: When? In 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yeah, early 1993. I'm not interested in the episode, but are you aware of the son being involved in some fracas or dispute with someone else, some customer, some drunken customer, which resulted in the drunken customer being hurt, the police coming around, and Mr. Tadic's son having to face court proceedings and being sentenced to a short period of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I know. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. That was early 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: One thing you do know though is that after a small and trivial incident in the Cafe AS the police responded, he was arrested, he was taken before a court, due process was observed, and he was sentenced to imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: The police did not react at all. As far as I know, there was no police. He only later on reported it to the police, who arrived and compiled this record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. That's all I want to know. I'm not interested in the episode at all. The episode itself is of no relevance to me at all. What I am interested in is the fact that something happened, police reacted, he was dealt with, he went to jail. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: He did not go to jail. Well, he wasn't sentenced. How should he then end up in a prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. But you're aware that something happened, that the police responded, the authorities somehow dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a regular procedure, I guess. It was the judiciary, the judiciary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Correct. That's right. That's right. It was the judiciary swinging into action and dealing with a minor offence. Correct.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if that same judiciary acted when prisoners were killed, murdered in the TO building or in the high school -- or in the high school gym? Are you aware of any paramilitaries being charged and taken off to prison, the police going round to visit them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of them having been killed there, at the TO and the other thing, so I also couldn't be aware of the procedure either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Then you know of an episode in Crkvina where 16 or 17 - perhaps my figures are wrong - but a large number of Croats were slaughtered in a warehouse? You know of that episode, in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the police --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: Everyone knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely right. And did the police swing into action as they did in the case of Mr. Tadic's son and arrest the malefactors?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. No, I know you weren't there. I understand that fully well. Did the information service in Bosanski Samac provide reports on any investigation that was in progress, to tell the people what was happening in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We had a radio station, but I rarely listened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions. I would only like to make a slight correction. The last answer by the witness was, "But I didn't listen to it, the radio."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the witness can repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your last answer to the question by the Prosecutor, concerning the radio. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: That I didn't listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bojic, I just have one -- a short question, and it's really just a clarification. On page 63, line 13 you were answering a question put to you by the Prosecutor, Mr. Di Fazio, concerning the 4th Detachment members and what they were doing at night. And your answer on line 13 was, "Not by night. The daytime. At night-time nobody took shifts." And I just wanted to be clear on this. Are you saying, as it seems to be, that the 4th Detachment was only guarding the perimeters of the town of Bosanski Samac on the embankments of the River Sava during the daytime and at night-time there were no shifts, everybody went home? That's what it seems to suggest. I would just like to --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would just like to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BOJIC
utterances.text: No. I wanted to say by saying this that there were no shifts during the night, meaning whoever was there in the evening stayed there until the morning. So -- but there was, of course, a 24-hour shift at the embankment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That's what I presumed. Because it seemed very odd that there wouldn't be anybody there at night. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojic, for giving evidence. We are now finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I would like to inform the Chamber that we have by finishing this witness, have finished with all the witnesses planned for the Defence case for Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and we have no further witnesses to call. But to use -- to seize this opportunity, the time that we have, since we know that there will be no other witness for the day, I still owe the Chamber to give them a translation of a document and another motion. So I would like to solve this issue now. So first of all, I would like to deliver to the Chamber translations of two documents. We received them beforehand, but I thought we -- it wasn't necessary to show them earlier because we had finished earlier. This is document D71/3 ID. This is an English translation of the list of civilians scheduled for the exchange who arrived from the Croatian side to be exchanged on the 4th of July, 1992. We had the B/C/S version. Now we have the English translation as well. And we give them to you in the order that we receive it from the translation service. If we could get a number now, unless there is an objection by the Prosecution, because we were just waiting for the translation. MR. DI FAZIO: No, there's no objection to this. And I believe there's another one, D72, that Mr. Lukic is going to tender, D72, which is also just a formal translation. And that can be done now too, and we've got no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So this document, D71/3, is now admitted into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next document, this is an official translation of the document D72/3 ID, the translation that we received in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This document, D72/3, is now admitted into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document I would like to tender as an exhibit is a document so far marked as D74/3 ID, which is a document I will remind the Chamber that I gave to Kemal Bobic during his testimony. And witness Gordana Pavlovic delivered this document from Belgrade and then it was delivered in the B/C/S form, in the B/C/S version. Now I have the official English translation and I would like to complete document with the English translation to be tendered as an exhibit. This is D74/3 ID. This is a contract -- a donation contract. This is the title, actually, of it. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: In respect of this particular document, the Prosecution view is that the threshold point for its admission has been reached because she testified about it in Belgrade. So no objection to its -- to its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Admission. MR. DI FAZIO: Admission. Its authenticity is, of course, another matter, and that will have to be assessed by you when you finally come to look at the evidence of Gordana Pavlovic and the other gentleman, now witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something, Your Honour, on the following issue: If the Court should find the authenticity of the document in dispute, I would ask of the Prosecution - because during the testimony of Kemal Bobic, if you remember when he was confronted with the document, the part of the document, he did not recognise it, so the document was merely marked for identification. But since Gordana Pavlovic recognised the entire document, I suggested that it be tendered as a whole. But if the Prosecution should contest the authenticity of the document, I will require the Prosecution to disclose to us the source of the -- the source that, delivered to them, the document that I confronted Kemal Bobic with. Since we received this document from the Prosecution, numbered 00604078, and I really am convinced that they received it from Kemal Bobic, I think that the Prosecution should speak up and say who they received this document from, the document that was disclosed to us by the Prosecution along with some other documents related to Kemal Bobic. Kemal Bobic told me that he had never seen the document and we received the document from the Prosecution, so we request the Prosecution to explain where they received this particular document from. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't want to embark into an analysis of the reliability or the authenticity of these documents. All I'm saying is I've got no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: But subject to later submissions, at the appropriate time on how you should view all of this evidence. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: There's plenty of documents that go in that are disputed by one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what matters is how much weight the Trial Chamber should attach to it. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In view of submissions made by the parties. MR. DI FAZIO: At a later point. At a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it will be admitted into evidence as D74/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is -- it's a binder of the communications centre. You remember that we marked the document for identification because there were two translations in the English language. This is D154/3 ID. We verified the -- both of the translations of this particular document of the communications centre. We came to the conclusion that there are some insignificant differences and that the translation we submit here to you is accurate. This is the internally marked by the number 00037299. This is the translation done from the original document and not from the photocopy, and I think we have already informed the Prosecution, Mr. Di Fazio, about it, and I think this is the translation that the Chamber should use when analysing this document. And since the identification number was there only for the verification of the translation, we hereby submit the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. D154/3 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender three lists of exchanges. I have mentioned them in my pre-trial brief, and I informed the Prosecution that we would be using them in the Defence case. I have talked to the Prosecution during the proceedings and I told them that I would introduce these documents at the end. These are seven documents. First is internally marked PDB71/3. This is the list of prisoner exchanges of 24th December, 1992. These are the persons who arrived for the exchange, as it says here, and this is -- this has both the B/C/S and the English version, so we would kindly tender this document. MR. DI FAZIO: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If these are lists of Serbs going into the municipality of Bosanski Samac? Yes. Could we just -- I don't have my copies right at hand. Might I have an opportunity just to have a look at them -- oh, no, I'm sorry. I'm informed my case manager has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: No, we've got no objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I just want to be clear. Maybe you said it already. This is the list of the Serbs who came from Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who came from -- through the Odzak commission, and at the time they were not able to be in Odzak. I just wanted to seize this opportunity to submit three lists of Serbs who were involved in the exchanges that we heard testimony about. So these were three exchanges. And we simply didn't have a chance of having any witnesses testifying about them, so I didn't have an opportunity to submit them at the time. And I am actually just using the proceedings that Ms. Aisling used to introduce these at the end of the case. So which -- how should this document be numbered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First, let's deal with PDB71/3, which we already have. That one is admitted into evidence. Can we have the number. I think it will be the next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As a completely new exhibit tendered in the order of the documents as we tendered them so far.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D187/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document, internally marked PDB62/3 is a list of persons who took part in the exchange on the 5th of November, 1992. This is what the document says. Although, there's a correction, that the exchange actually took place on the 7th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D188/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document is another list of exchanged persons, marked PDB57/3. This is a list of persons arriving from Bosanski Brod on the 5th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D189/3 and ter for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next documents that I have prepared are all contained in the pre-trial brief of Mr. Tadic. We said that we would use them in the presentation of evidence, and they relate to the international documents by different authors talking about the exchange of prisoners, and this is relevant for the indictment and the time frame. It's internally marked PDB143/3. This is the agreement number 2 of the International Red Cross in Geneva, signed by participants - I won't mention them here - of 23rd May, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: In the interests of economy of time and so on, may I ask that Mr. Lukic deal with this on another day. I'm well aware of the documents that he's -- he's referring to, and he has kindly offered -- sorry, given copies to the Prosecution. The problem is that I haven't yet had a chance to confer with my colleagues over this -- this documentation. I would like on opportunity to do so. It may be that there will be no objection to the admission into evidence of these documents, but if I can be provided with some more time, a day or two, that will give me an opportunity to discuss it with Mr. Weiner and with Mr. Re. We may be able to resolve the issue or at least focus the issue a bit more carefully. But I just haven't had that opportunity yet. So I'd ask that we deal with these documents on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has explained that they are referred to in the pre-trial brief. The only question I have to ask him is: When were they actually given to the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: They were given to us - I can't recall - now but some days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you had enough -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say, Your Honours, I did not want to take up the time of the trial and of the witnesses. I really waited for this stage to be over. All these documents were contained in the pre-trial brief and were given to the Prosecution then. And then a week ago - I will tell you specifically when - this was before the testimony by Mr. Tadic, that I gave them these documents because we then said that I would wait for some free time to show up to tender them into evidence, but I really think we should use up the time we have today to deal with these technical issues to include them in the documentation. But if it's not possible, we would wait for the Prosecution to give their reply. MR. DI FAZIO: We can do it tomorrow, if Your Honours please. Essentially the issue is very simple: That's one of a series of Red Cross documents dealing with issues of exchanges. The Prosecution may be able to locate other Red Cross documents, and it may be that it might be more helpful to you if you saw the series in its entirety rather than an individual document. All we, the Prosecution, need is some time to confer amongst itself and gather those documents together, examine them in a little more detail, and it may be that then there will be no objection at all to the documents' admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honours, this is a completely different issue. I would like to tender those -- the evidence that we have mentioned in our pre-trial brief and in our presentation of the case. Now, if the -- what the Prosecutor says, within the meaning of Rule 85, this could come under a completely different procedure, and this has nothing to do with what we had already planned in our pre-trial brief to be tendered, apart from that, in agreement with Rule 65(G) they didn't object to these documents in the pre-trial procedure when we were writing our pre-trial brief, and they were informed about it. I don't object to the Prosecution giving their objections later on, but these two different types of evidence cannot run hand in hand because these are -- this is evidence we have announced beforehand and what the Prosecutor is mentioning now is new evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very simply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: David Re, who is a member of our trial team, is handling this matter. I can't respond in any of the Red Cross documents. Mr. Di Fazio can't respond in any of those Red Cross documents. I looked at them a month or so ago. I don't recall them. David Re is taking up this matter. We can take it up first thing in the morning. I don't see any problem with any of them when I look at them, but he's handling the matter. It would be much easier for him to handle it. If we knew that they were going to discuss this today, I'd have Mr. Re down here. If you want to take a break now, it's at the hour and a half mark, I can try and find Mr. Re and see if he's in the building. But at this point I can't respond to it, Mr. Di Fazio can't respond it to it, and we weren't prepared to respond to it today. I didn't receive any notice yesterday that this matter would be on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, and as we won't have witnesses all day tomorrow, we can have some time tomorrow to discuss the issue in the presence of the learned colleague who is informed about these documents. Since we will close for today, I would like to seize this opportunity to mention another issue relating to these documents now that we have our colleague binder here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a break and resume our proceedings at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has to decide on the documents. Do you want to say anything further, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I can help out. We met at the break. We have no problem with the Red Cross document. Counsel can tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the other documents that they have too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I continue. The first document that I wish to tender now is a document that is internally marked PDB143/3. I'm going to call the document Agreement Number 2 before the International Red Cross dated the 23rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D190/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is a document that is internally marked PDB67/3. I'm going to call it UNPROFOR's proposal for the mutual release of prisoners. This is a document that does not have a date, but you will easily see that in paragraph 6 reference is made to the period when it was actually adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D191/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document is the document that was internally marked PDB69/3. I'm going to call it the Agreement from Budapest dated the 16th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D192/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next document is a document internally marked PDB136/3. I shall call it Principles and procedures regulating the mediation of International Red Cross in exchanges. Just a moment, please. There is a date here. The document is dated the 24th of July, 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: The title, if Your Honours please, is somewhat of a misnomer, or at least the way it was translated, I don't know. The document itself is headed "Guidelines on principles and procedures for the ICRC involvement in operations of release and exchange." That might be -- I take that from the English, and I think that might be a more accurate description of the exhibit, and the Prosecution would be happier with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we shall take the one on the English as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- as the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I can also inform the Trial Chamber of the following: This document is officially in English, but the translation that you have been given is the one that was sent to the relevant office, I believe, in Zagreb, but that's why we gave it to you in that form. And the last document that the Defence wishes to tender into evidence -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D193/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document that the Defence of Miroslav Tadic wishes to tender into evidence is the document that was internally marked PDB147/3. This is part of the Dayton Paris Peace Agreement, Annex 1A. I have singled out only one thing, and I believe that that is the only thing that is of interest. Only Article 9. But if necessary, we can tender the entire annex. So I have submitted the first page to you so that the source of the document could be seen. And what I'm particularly interested in is Article 9, which is entitled "Exchange of prisoners." MR. DI FAZIO: The document that the Prosecution was given, if Your Honours please, was -- consisted of Article 1 -- I'm sorry. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. I have nothing to say on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D194/3 and ter for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By this document we have concluded the tendering of documents. I would just like to deal with two other matters that we still have to address the Trial Chamber about, and I think that for one document -- or rather, one matter we have to speak together, the OTP and us, and then the other one is different. If you remember, D153/3 -- 155/3, that is the HVO order on the withdrawal of the military and the population from the territory of Odzak. When Miroslav Tadic testified, I introduced that. And Mr. Di Fazio then said that he accepts that but he said that he is contesting the authenticity of it. And then I asked him to give us the reasons why they were challenging it, because I wanted to apply Rule 89(D) if the authenticity of this document is being contested. So then the Trial Chamber told us that the parties should discuss this between themselves. I talked to my colleagues from the OTP, and they said that they can state their views regarding that document, whether they continue to challenge its authenticity and whether it can therefore be tendered at all, and also so that I would know how to deal with it, whether I have to prove the facts related to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is D153/3 or D155/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is D155/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection to its being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It can be admitted into evidence. I hear that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand it's already an exhibit, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes. The Prosecution did not object to that, but it was only the authenticity that was questioned. But now they no longer question it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, they are no longer questioning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still owe the Trial Chamber one more thing, and that is the official translation of a document. That is the decision on the appointment of Svetozar Vasovic in the Red Cross. The translation was controversial and Mr. David Re and I are still awaiting a new version of the translation, so we are going to state our views when the OTP receives a new translation because there were some different interpretations as to his appointment to the Red Cross. So I believe that in this way, we have honoured all our obligations vis-a-vis the Trial Chamber and we have dealt with all of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The document you are referring to, I think, is D143? Because it's no use discussing without recording the number. But it was never marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Was it given an identification number or not, the appointment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. It was admitted, and there was just one thing that we had to agree upon, that is, the translation of one sentence. So it's not the document that is questionable but it's just one sentence. If you'll recall, whether Mr. Vasovic was employed in the Red Cross or whether he was volunteering there. We are waiting for the translation service to define that for us. I think that the entire document has been admitted into evidence and that it no longer has an ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For purposes of having a clear record, perhaps once the parties have discussed this, we may refer to this page of the transcript so that we identify the number of the document. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood this correctly, once the document arrives, then we are going to recall today's discussion concerning it. Did I understand it properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Discussion, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic received the English translations of witness statements that were provided under 92 bis yesterday afternoon. I have given copies of the translation to the Office of the Prosecutor immediately, so I would now like to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Judge Lindholm wishes to raise a matter before you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. A question to Mr. Lukic in order to be certain that I haven't missed anything and haven't mixed up things. I still have some documents in the sea of documents marked with PDB, and I would like to ask you whether they are now obsolete or whether they are -- I have missed something. I will repeat the numbers very slowly: 19/3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's PDB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: They are all PDB. So 19/3, 23/3, 72/3, and 81/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Lindholm, I just know that at any rate we gave up or some documents that we had originally intended to tender. I am going to check these particular documents, and I'm going to tell you tomorrow whether these documents did indeed become exhibits or whether we gave up on these documents altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, this is the last batch, is it? This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be treated as document D174/1 ID and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask that we state that this is Witness Lazar Mirkic's statement. I would like this to be in the transcript. [In English] Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because then there is no confusion as to whose statement it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Statement of Cvijetic Dusanka will be treated as document D175/1 and ter for the B/C/S. The statement of Branislav Marisic will be treated as document D176/1 ter ID and D176/1 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe just to assist the Registry. Here in the transcript we have for document D175/1 and ter for the B/C/S there is no ID mark, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I did say and ter for the B/C/S. This is at line 22. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, if I could just say to the registrar, that Mr. Lazarevic was not talking about the ter; he was talking about the ID mark. That's on line -- line 3 of page 86.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll repeat the document. It is a document that's ID and is D175/1 ID and ter for the B/C/S ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber expects the Prosecution to indicate their position on these three statements under the provisions of Rule 92 bis by 13.00 hours Monday. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. That will be done. And may I seek just a clarification. Is that to be -- can that be done orally, or do you want it in the form of a motion? May I say that the Prosecution would prefer to do it orally. But we'll obviously -- if the Chamber wishes a written motion, then we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber prefers to have it in writing. It's much easier. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. And that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: That will be done by Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There was one matter the Prosecution -- the Trial Chamber wanted the Prosecution's position. Mr. Pantelic had applied to withdraw a witness, Mr. Cedomir Simic, who had given a statement under Rule 92 bis, and the Prosecution wished to be heard. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. We don't have any objection to the withdrawal of the witness, and of course that means a withdrawal of his statement and any material provided by him, and that will not -- that material will not be evidence in the proceedings at all. And of course, on that basis, the Prosecution has no objection to the withdrawal of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will give its ruling in due course. Yes. What is the position regarding witnesses for Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were informed by the Victim and Witness Section that Ms. Fatima Zaric has arrived this morning in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I can't hear you. Would you speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best. Ms. Zaric has arrived in The Hague and we were informed in that respect about -- from the Victim and Witness Section. Hopefully she will be able to start her testimony tomorrow. I still haven't had the opportunity to see her and see how she feels. I spoke with her yesterday in the afternoon about her arrival. She said that she's under some sort of influenza, that she's not feeling too good but hopefully she will get better and start her testimony tomorrow. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After Ms. Zaric -- Mrs. Zaric, sorry, we have three more witnesses that are arriving in The Hague tomorrow and another one that will arrive in The Hague on Saturday. And also -- well, because of certain problems with this witness - he is afraid of flying in the airplane, he had to come by his own car, and he will be here on Saturday - and the last group will also come on Saturday by plane. So we will have all our witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Zaric will testify tomorrow, because she's -- she's quite brief. Part of her testimony is under the statement already, isn't it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. We shall adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow.
